name: Nose reshaping clip

lead: A nose reshaping clip, also sold as a nose shaper or lifter, is a soft plastic or silicone device fitted onto the nose and worn for periods of time. People use it hoping for a higher tip, a narrower bridge or a straighter nose without surgery.

The claim is that sustained gentle pressure can retrain nasal cartilage over time. No controlled trial of such clips for the adult nose has been identified; the nearest research covers nasal molding appliances used under clinical supervision, which work on soft infant cartilage, and non-surgical rhinoplasty with hyaluronic acid filler.

paras: Users wear the device for hours at a time, often while at home or asleep, as an inexpensive alternative to rhinoplasty. Marketing promises gradual change over weeks of regular wear.

Risks are skin irritation, pressure marks and breathing discomfort. Adult nasal cartilage and bone are rigid, and cosmetic changes to the nose are usually assessed by a surgeon. Nose clips in medicine are studied for unrelated uses such as controlling nosebleeds.

chain: Clip presses on nose for hours
angle.text: Users clip the nose for hours hoping to lift the tip or narrow the bridge as an alternative to rhinoplasty. The idea is that steady pressure gradually reshapes cartilage; clinical studies cover infant molding and filler, not these clips.

lead: A nose reshaping clip, also sold as a nose shaper, lifter or slimmer, is a soft plastic or silicone device that is clipped or fitted onto the nose and worn for periods of time. It is marketed as a non-surgical way to lift the tip, narrow the bridge or straighten the nose.

No controlled trial of such clips for reshaping the adult nose has been identified. The nearest published research concerns two different interventions: nasal molding appliances used under clinical supervision in reconstructive settings, and non-surgical rhinoplasty with hyaluronic acid filler.[1][2] Nose clips are also studied in medicine for unrelated purposes, such as compression to control nosebleeds and as laboratory breathing aids.[3]
Proponents say sustained gentle pressure can retrain nasal cartilage over time; researchers have not tested this for commercial clips.
infobox: Silicone or plastic nasal clip or splint
Nose shaper, nose lifter, nose slimmer

paras: Commercial products vary from small U-shaped silicone clips that pinch the nasal sides, to bridge-shaping pads and strap-supported lifters worn at night. Brands generally recommend wearing them for set periods daily, and promotional material often shows before-and-after photographs.

In clinics, external and intranasal molding appliances are used as a non-surgical adjunct in nasal reconstruction. A retrospective review of 42 patients treated with one institution's molding approach reported that anthropometric ratios of the columella and alar sidewall moved towards normative values after a mean molding duration of about six months. This was a conference abstract describing an uncontrolled retrospective series, and the appliances were clinician-designed.[2]
Such studies concern medical appliances managed by specialists and do not establish that over-the-counter clips produce comparable changes.
No studies found of nose reshaping clips for cosmetic nasal change in adults.

A 2024 systematic review of non-surgical rhinoplasty, mostly with hyaluronic acid filler, included 16 studies (none randomized). It reported that about 93 percent of 652 treated patients were satisfied, that results typically lasted 8 to 12 months, and that most complications were minor, with rarer serious ones such as skin necrosis or vascular occlusion. Filler injection is not comparable to wearing an external clip.[1]

A 2018 randomized trial compared a nose clip with manual compression for managing nosebleeds, and other studies use nose clips for breathing measurements and exercise physiology. These studies do not address appearance.[3]

Plausible risks of external nasal devices include skin irritation, pressure marks and reduced comfort in breathing through the nose when worn. No safety data for cosmetic shaping clips have been published.

Nose clips are discussed as an inexpensive alternative to rhinoplasty. Those who use them report subjective changes in tip position or bridge width, usually shown with photographs; no controlled measurement exists. Surgeons and reviewers describe non-surgical changes to the nasal framework as limited to what filler or surgical techniques can achieve.[1]
